inserts.title: Stimulus spacing sets the size of the decrement
paragraphs: The decrement in gill withdrawal depends on how the repeated siphon stimuli are spaced in time. Pinsker and colleagues held the seawater-jet stimulus constant and varied the interval between stimuli, so the spacing alone sets the pattern of repetition in each series.

Shorter intervals produced a faster decline in contraction, while longer intervals slowed it. Responses commonly fell toward about 25% of the initial amplitude across the range of intervals tested. Each series begins from the same first response in the same animal.

Stimuli delivered at closer intervals leave less time for the response to recover between trials. Recovery between trials is therefore part of what determines how far responsiveness falls across a series.

inserts.title: Skin stimuli evoke EPSPs in an identified motor neuron
paragraphs: An identified gill motor neuron receives a direct excitatory input from the skin of the siphon. Brief stimuli to that skin depolarize the motor cell, and this depolarization is the first measurable link between touch and contraction.

Castellucci and colleagues recorded the response in the same cell on repeated trials. Repeated stimulation reduced the response, and the reduction accumulated from one trial to the next across each session.
Each EPSP in the identified cell can be traced to one defined synapse. The cell's large size makes it possible to record that synapse repeatedly over the whole session.

inserts.title: Shock acts on sensory inputs beyond the tapped one
paragraphs: Antonov and colleagues recorded behavior and neural activity together through a set of training protocols. Habituation used repeated siphon taps, dishabituation added tail shock after habituation, and sensitization used shock alone.

Facilitation appeared in sensory neurons whose receptive fields covered the test site and in sensory neurons activated from elsewhere on the body. The modulatory action of shock therefore reaches more inputs than the one that was tapped during habituation.
The change is spread across many connections, so its synaptic basis appears at several sites. Motor-cell firing, complex postsynaptic potentials and monosynaptic potentials each track this spread.

inserts.title: Strong and weak connections depress at similar rates
paragraphs: Gover and colleagues evoked sensory action potentials at 15 s intervals in strong and weak sensory–motor connections. The two kinds of connection differed in their initial transmission and in their paired-pulse behavior, yet they depressed at similar rates.

Applying 4-aminopyridine broadened sensory spikes and increased calcium-dependent release. This change raised initial transmission while depression stayed the same speed, which is the opposite of what a simple depletion account would predict.

The observed depression kinetics therefore point to silencing of functional release sites in a stimulus-dependent way. Activity itself drives the silencing rather than the strength of the initial connection.

inserts.title: Spaced training retains more than massed training
paragraphs: Carew and colleagues gave forty habituation trials in one day to one group, and the same total spread over four days to another. The **massed** schedule concentrated the experience in one session, and the **spaced** schedule distributed it across days.

Both schedules produced substantial decrement during training. Spaced training yielded stronger retention after 24 h and after one week than massed training. The response within a single session predicts little about how much of the change lasts across days.

Retention was measured as withdrawal behavior, and it could be tested in a restrained preparation as well. Spacing effects of this kind set up the later experiments that examine the molecular events under different temporal patterns.

inserts.title: Serotonin enhances EPSPs after depression
paragraphs: Brunelli and colleagues compared serotonin, dopamine and octopamine at the sensory-neuron connection onto a gill motor neuron. Serotonin changes how an existing pathway responds, so the same connection can be measured before and after each neuromodulator.

Sensory neurons were first depressed by repeated stimulation. Serotonin applied during a 2.5 min rest increased the subsequent synaptic responses. Rest periods without serotonin produced no such enhancement, so the drug accounts for the increase.

The antagonist cinanserin reversibly reduced the facilitation evoked by connective stimulation, while the repeated-stimulation depression stayed intact. This pattern identifies a serotonergic route to facilitation that runs alongside the depression.

inserts.title: Type 2 PKA concentrates near nerve endings
paragraphs: Liu and colleagues measured PKA regulatory subunits in cell bodies, neurites and synaptosomes, which are terminal-enriched particles isolated from nervous tissue. Type 1 PKA was mostly soluble, whereas type 2 PKA was enriched in neuronal processes and tied to anchoring proteins near nerve endings.

Repeated serotonin treatment increased RII protein in synaptosome preparations at 24 h. Immunostaining also detected more RII in sensory neurons. Prolonged facilitation is therefore linked to a change in the amount and location of a signaling protein, not only to a brief rise in cAMP.
Each synaptosome preparation contains many terminals, so the measured increase is an average across them. Nuclear type 1 PKA and synaptic type 2 PKA carry complementary roles in this account.

inserts.title: Postsynaptic calcium contributes to facilitation
paragraphs: Li and colleagues introduced BAPTA, a fast calcium buffer, into the motor neuron of cultured sensory–motor synapses. Intracellular calcium regulates signaling inside a cell without being the extracellular transmitter. The buffer therefore tests whether facilitation needs a change beyond the sensory terminal.

A ten-minute application of 10 μM serotonin enhanced control EPSPs. Buffering postsynaptic calcium reduced the facilitation, most clearly after serotonin was removed. Motor-cell injections without the buffer showed that the effect comes from the calcium buffer itself.

Facilitation therefore needs a postsynaptic calcium signal in this preparation. A single connection can change on both sides at once, so the presynaptic and postsynaptic results combine into one account.

inserts.title: Motor-cell toxin blocks dishabituation
paragraphs: Li and colleagues moved the postsynaptic toxin experiment from culture into a reduced siphon-withdrawal preparation. Identified motor neurons were injected with botulinum toxin B before a sequence of siphon taps, tail shock and further siphon tests.

inserts.title: Synthesis is needed during a restricted window
paragraphs: Montarolo and colleagues varied when anisomycin was present relative to repeated serotonin. A three-hour exposure during and immediately after induction blocked long-term facilitation. Inhibition that began much earlier, or several hours later, left the 24 h enhancement intact.

Biochemical measurements showed strong suppression of protein synthesis during drug exposure and recovery after washout. The timing of the drug therefore lines up with its effect on the cell. Long-term facilitation depends on new synthesis during a restricted induction period.
A critical window fits the production of proteins that start or stabilize persistent change. The identities, turnover rates and locations of these proteins are the next questions.

inserts.title: CREB1 binds the synapsin promoter
paragraphs: **CREB1** is a transcription factor that regulates gene expression by binding DNA. A **promoter** is a DNA region that controls transcription of a gene. Hart and colleagues identified a cAMP response element in the _Aplysia_ synapsin promoter, which is a site that CREB1 can bind.

A promoter-driven fluorescent reporter increased expression after serotonin treatment. Chromatin immunoprecipitation, which pulls down DNA bound to a chosen protein, found more CREB1 bound to the synapsin promoter. These measurements link the regulatory sequence, transcription-factor binding and expression level.
Serotonin-dependent signaling reaches synapsin production through CREB1 binding at this promoter. Other transcriptional responses of long-term facilitation are assigned to their own target genes.

2: _Aplysia californica_ is a marine gastropod whose siphon carries water out of the mantle cavity, the chamber that holds its respiratory gill. Touching the siphon or the adjacent mantle shelf evokes contraction of the gill, siphon and mantle shelf. **Withdrawal** shields these delicate structures from the disturbing stimulus, which is the defensive function of the reflex.

Pinsker and colleagues held animals with the gill exposed and delivered seawater jets through a nozzle. A photocell read gill movement from light scattered by the tissue. Jets lasted about 800 ms, and stronger jets produced larger contractions followed by additional delayed components.

Stimulus intensity and response amplitude can be measured separately in this preparation. Because the jet strength sets the size of the contraction, the same animal can be tested across a range of intensities.
3: **Habituation** is a decrease in responsiveness caused by repeated presentation of a stimulus. Pinsker and colleagues stimulated the same siphon receptive region again and again with the same jet. The gill contracted less on each trial, even though the jet kept reaching the animal at full strength.

Responses fell toward roughly 25% of the first amplitude when stimuli arrived at intervals ranging from seconds to several minutes. Longer intervals slowed the decline. The number of stimuli needed for a given decrement therefore depends on how the trials are spaced in time.

A smaller contraction alone can arise from sensory adaptation, weaker central transmission, altered motor-neuron firing or muscle fatigue. Intracellular recordings in the same preparation sort these sites.
4: **Spontaneous recovery** is the return of responsiveness after stimulation stops. In the gill-withdrawal experiments, a previously effective stimulus again produced a substantial contraction after a rest. A recovered response can decline again during a new series of identical stimuli.

Recovery had two phases. Pinsker and colleagues described a rapid component over about 10–20 min that accounted for roughly 75–85% of the recovery, followed by a slower component. Some animals recovered fully within 10 min, while others were still incompletely recovered at 122 min.

The animal keeps the capacity to contract its gill throughout habituation. Recovery of this kind points to a reversible change rather than to injury or to failure of the muscles, so the decrement lies in the control of the response.
5: **Dishabituation** is an increase in a previously habituated response after a different, stronger stimulus. Pinsker and colleagues first reduced gill withdrawal with repeated siphon stimulation, then applied a strong tactile stimulus to another part of the body. The original test stimulus then evoked larger contractions again.

The increase lasted several minutes and could exceed the original response level. **Sensitization** is an increased responsiveness that follows a strong or noxious stimulus, so it can be superimposed on the response that habituation reduced. The restored movement shows that the depressed response is reversible.

The same siphon test stimulus was used before and after the strong stimulus, so the test input stayed constant while the modulatory event changed. The result requires a process that raises defensive responsiveness across several inputs at once.
6: Castellucci and colleagues isolated the abdominal ganglion, a cluster of neuronal cell bodies, and kept a siphon nerve and its attached receptive skin. A **sensory neuron** detects stimulation of that skin, and a **motor neuron** drives contraction of a peripheral muscle. The large identified cells in this ganglion allowed repeated intracellular recordings.

Brief mechanical or electrical skin stimuli produced an excitatory postsynaptic potential, or EPSP, in an identified gill motor neuron, usually L7. An EPSP is a membrane depolarization that moves a neuron toward the threshold for an action potential. Repeated stimulation reduced this response from one trial to the next.

The isolated ganglion contains a defined sensory–motor pathway, so the connection can be recorded directly. Relating these neural changes to the behavior of the whole animal requires recordings from more intact preparations.
7: A **monosynaptic connection** links a presynaptic neuron directly to a postsynaptic neuron through one synapse. Castellucci and colleagues raised the concentration of divalent ions to suppress most polysynaptic activity, then recorded elementary EPSPs in a gill motor neuron.

The EPSPs had a short, stable latency, and their amplitude fell during repeated stimulation. The decrement persisted when the motor neuron was hyperpolarized to reduce spontaneous inhibitory potentials. Direct stimulation of the connective also produced the decrement, which places the change in the connection rather than in the stimulated skin.

The change therefore occurs within central excitatory transmission at this synapse. A sensory action potential can still arrive at full size while the postsynaptic response is smaller, because the effectiveness of transmission has changed.
8: Antonov and colleagues combined intracellular recordings with siphon-movement measurements in a reduced preparation. **LFS motor neurons** are identified output cells for siphon withdrawal, and **LE sensory neurons** supply tactile input. Stimulating one LFS neuron artificially made it possible to compare its contribution with the withdrawal evoked by touch.

The contribution of a single LFS neuron grew with its firing rate. Measurements of movement, complex postsynaptic potentials and individual sensory–motor EPSPs indicate that the LE-to-LFS monosynaptic pathway mediates about one-third of the measured reflex. Other circuit and peripheral mechanisms supply the rest.

Activating the motor cell directly skips sensory processing, so downstream changes can be isolated from changes at the sensory input. The one-third estimate describes siphon flaring in this preparation.
9: Antonov and colleagues recorded siphon withdrawal, LFS motor-neuron firing, LE sensory-neuron firing and synaptic potentials during behavioral training. Habituation used repeated siphon taps, dishabituation added tail shock after habituation, and sensitization used shock alone.

Withdrawal, motor-cell firing, complex postsynaptic potentials and monosynaptic sensory–motor potentials usually changed together. Facilitation appeared in sensory neurons whose receptive fields covered the test site and in sensory neurons activated from elsewhere on the body. Shock therefore acts on more inputs than the one tapped during habituation.

The change is spread across many connections, so its synaptic basis appears at several sites. Transient inhibition in the siphon preparation is absent from the gill preparation, which means the apparent difference between dishabituation and sensitization depends on the reflex component measured.
10: Castellucci and Kandel analyzed sensory–motor transmission when transmitter release was low. A **quantum** is the postsynaptic effect of one unit of transmitter release, usually interpreted as the contents of one vesicle. Low calcium and high magnesium increased transmission failures and made small successful responses easier to resolve.

They evoked sensory spikes repeatedly and recorded motor-neuron EPSPs. The amplitudes alternated between failures and small responses, while the overall response shrank during depression. Successive periods of transmission showed whether fewer quanta were released or whether the motor neuron responded less to each quantum.

This approach gives a functional estimate of release, not a direct view of vesicle fusion. The estimate rests on resolving single-quantum responses and on the statistical model of release, and the altered ionic bath changes the conditions relative to an intact animal.
11: During synaptic depression, Castellucci and Kandel found a decrease in **quantal content**, the average number of transmitter quanta released per sensory impulse. The estimated size of one quantum stayed nearly constant. Less transmitter reached the motor neuron even while the sensory neuron was being stimulated.

Averaged successful EPSPs kept a similar time course during depression, while failures became more common. A constant quantum size points to a presynaptic change in this short-term preparation, not to a large loss of postsynaptic receptor sensitivity. The main measured change sits on the presynaptic side of the synapse.

Fewer released quanta can arise from vesicle depletion, a lower release probability or fewer available release sites. Quantal analysis identifies the side of the synapse that changes most strongly under these conditions, and the specific mechanism is identified by separate experiments.
12: **Homosynaptic depression** is reduced transmission caused by activity in the same synaptic pathway. Gover and colleagues evoked sensory action potentials at 15 s intervals in strong and weak sensory–motor connections. The two kinds of connection differed in their initial transmission and in their paired-pulse behavior, yet they depressed at similar rates.

The **paired-pulse ratio** compares the postsynaptic responses to two closely spaced presynaptic spikes. Applying 2 mM 4-aminopyridine, a potassium-channel blocker, broadened sensory spikes and increased calcium-dependent release. This change shifted initial transmission and paired-pulse behavior, but depression was not faster as a simple depletion account would predict.

Depression follows its own time course, independent of the initial strength of a connection. Activity appears to silence functional release sites in a stimulus-dependent way, and the measured kinetics are the evidence for that account.
13: Gover and colleagues induced homosynaptic depression with repeated sensory-neuron stimulation, then left the connection unstimulated for 40 min. Subsequent EPSPs stayed depressed instead of returning to their original amplitude. A shorter rest interval produced recovery of a different size, which marks the depression as persistent rather than immediate.

Motor-neuron responsiveness and sensory-cell stimulation stayed measurable throughout the rest. With the release-manipulation results, the persistence favors a change in the availability of functional release sites over a simple exhausted pool that refills quickly at rest.

Recovery in intact animals takes place over a different time course, because stimulus history, ionic conditions and network contributions all differ from the isolated connection. The 40 min persistence is a property of this synapse under these conditions.
14: **Long-term habituation** is a reduction in responsiveness that is retained beyond the training session. Carew and colleagues trained unrestrained animals with ten siphon-stimulation trials per day for four days. An observer timed withdrawal duration without knowing each animal's training group.

Trained animals responded less than controls when tested after 24 h and after one week. Reduced responsiveness was still detectable after three weeks, although some recovery had occurred. Gill-withdrawal tests in a restrained preparation also showed retention, so the effect extends to the gill component as well.

Retention lasting weeks indicates that a simple withdrawal system supports enduring nonassociative learning. The retained change could rest on persistent synaptic efficacy, on altered connectivity or on changes elsewhere in the circuit.
15: Carew and colleagues gave forty habituation trials in one day to one group and the same total spread over four days to another. The **massed** schedule concentrated the experience in one session, and the **spaced** schedule separated the sessions by day.

Both schedules produced substantial decrement during training. Spaced training yielded stronger retention after 24 h and after one week than massed training. The response within a single session therefore predicts little about how much of the change persists across days.

The measured outcome is withdrawal behavior, not protein synthesis or synapse number. Spacing effects of this kind lead to later experiments that test the molecular events under different temporal patterns.
16: Bailey and Chen filled identified sensory neurons with horseradish peroxidase, an enzyme that reveals cell processes, and reconstructed the labeled arbors after behavioral training. A **varicosity** is an axonal swelling that can contain presynaptic release machinery. Counting varicosities gave a measure of connectivity in trained and control animals.

Control neurons in the habituation experiment averaged 1,291 varicosities, whereas neurons from long-term habituated animals averaged 836. In the sensitization experiment the averages were 1,320 for controls and 2,697 for sensitized animals. Persistent decrement and persistent enhancement therefore produce changes in opposite directions.

The counts describe labeled structures in the arbor rather than transmitter release at each swelling. A changed varicosity count accompanies the remembered response, and the individual swellings that carry the change are identified separately.
17: Frost and colleagues trained intact animals for long-term sensitization, then recorded identified sensory–motor connections in isolated abdominal ganglia. Sensitization increases defensive responsiveness after strong stimulation, without requiring a predictive relation between two stimuli.

Monosynaptic EPSPs onto the gill motor neuron L7 were larger in trained animals than in controls. Baseline motor-cell membrane properties were measured as well, which distinguishes increased synaptic input from a general rise in postsynaptic resistance. The recorded connection therefore keeps a trace of the earlier behavioral experience.

The ganglion preparation removes the ongoing behavioral context, while the enhanced synapse persists in it. Interneurons, other motor cells and peripheral targets could carry further parts of the sensitization.
18: Brunelli and colleagues compared serotonin, dopamine and octopamine at the sensory-neuron connection onto a gill motor neuron. **Serotonin**, also called 5-hydroxytryptamine or 5-HT, is a neuromodulator that changes how an existing pathway responds, rather than conveying the tactile test stimulus itself.

Sensory neurons were stimulated fifteen times at 10 s intervals to depress their EPSPs. Serotonin applied during a 2.5 min rest increased the synaptic responses that followed. In the published results, 2 μM and 100 μM serotonin both produced facilitation, while rest periods without serotonin produced no such enhancement.

The antagonist cinanserin reversibly reduced the facilitation evoked by connective stimulation, and the depression produced by repeated stimulation was unchanged. This pattern identifies a serotonergic route to facilitation that is separate from the depression itself.
19: **Cyclic AMP**, or cAMP, is an intracellular second messenger that links receptor activation to downstream responses. Brunelli and colleagues applied a membrane-permeant cAMP analog and injected cAMP directly into sensory-neuron cell bodies. Both treatments enhanced the EPSPs recorded in the postsynaptic motor neurons.

Rest alone, comparable current injection, cyclic GMP and 5′-AMP each failed to reproduce the cAMP enhancement. Injected cAMP increased transmission without changing the amplitude or duration of the action potential recorded at the sensory cell body. Synaptic efficacy therefore changed while the spike at the cell body stayed the same.

Spike propagation and calcium entry at distant terminals could still change with cAMP. Those possibilities are tested by recordings at the terminals themselves, which identify the compartment where cAMP acts.
20: **Protein kinase A**, or PKA, transfers phosphate groups onto target proteins when cAMP activates it. Its regulatory subunits hold the catalytic subunits in check, and cAMP binding releases that inhibition. Liu and colleagues distinguished type 1 and type 2 PKA by their regulatory subunits and their cellular distributions.

**A-kinase anchoring proteins**, or AKAPs, hold type 2 PKA in place by binding its RII regulatory subunit. The Ht31 peptide blocks this binding. Ht31 reduced serotonin-induced short-term and long-term facilitation, whereas an inactive control peptide did not.

Kinase activity must be available near the right targets, so the location of PKA is part of the mechanism. The Ht31 result shows that localized PKA signaling is needed for facilitation in this sensorimotor preparation.
21: Liu and colleagues compared PKA regulatory subunits in cell bodies, neurites and synaptosomes, which are terminal-enriched particles isolated from nervous tissue. Type 1 PKA was mostly soluble, whereas type 2 PKA was enriched in neuronal processes and associated with anchoring proteins near nerve endings.

Repeated serotonin treatment increased RII protein in synaptosome preparations at 24 h. Immunostaining also detected more RII in sensory neurons. Prolonged facilitation is therefore tied to a change in the amount and location of a signaling protein, not only to a short rise in cAMP.

Each synaptosome preparation contains many terminals, so the measured increase is an average across them. The nuclear type 1 and synaptic type 2 PKA pools were assigned complementary roles from the biochemical and physiological data together.
22: Liu and colleagues asked whether increased RII expression is required for long-term facilitation or only accompanies it. **Antisense oligonucleotides** are short nucleic-acid sequences designed to bind a target RNA and reduce its expression. They were injected into sensory neurons before repeated serotonin treatment.

RII antisense reduced the serotonin-induced rise in RII protein and impaired facilitation measured 24 h later. Control injections and manipulations of the other regulatory-subunit class showed that the effect depends on the RII target rather than on injection itself. Electrophysiology and protein measurements were taken from the same cells.

Transcription, translation, anchoring and other signaling pathways act alongside RII in this protocol. Knocking down RII therefore shows that RII is required for this form of facilitation, and the rest of the mechanism is built around that requirement.
23: Dale and Kandel compared sensory-neuron-evoked currents with motor-neuron responses to applied L-glutamate, an amino-acid neurotransmitter. Voltage-clamp recordings held the motor cell at set membrane potentials and measured synaptic current, which isolates voltage dependence from changes in the firing threshold.

Evoked transmission and glutamate responses shared voltage-dependent and pharmacological properties. Magnesium suppressed a component at negative voltages, which fits a channel block relieved by depolarization. The authors judged glutamate a likely fast excitatory transmitter, and they noted that applied agonist responses differ from naturally released transmitter.

**Ionotropic receptors** open an ion channel directly when a transmitter binds. The resulting current depolarizes the motor cell and can recruit spikes that drive withdrawal muscles. Matching pharmacology supports glutamate as the transmitter, and the vesicle contents themselves are measured by other methods.
24: Li and colleagues tested cultured sensory–motor synapses while introducing **BAPTA**, a fast calcium buffer, into the motor neuron. Intracellular calcium regulates signaling inside a cell without being the extracellular transmitter. Introducing the buffer into the postsynaptic cell tests whether facilitation needs a change beyond the sensory terminal.

A ten-minute application of 10 μM serotonin enhanced control EPSPs. Buffering postsynaptic calcium reduced the facilitation, most clearly after serotonin was removed. Motor-cell injections without the buffer and test-only conditions showed that the effect arises from the calcium buffer rather than from recording or repeated testing.

Facilitation therefore needs a postsynaptic calcium signal in this preparation. The quantal and cAMP results from the sensory side remain valid, and a single connection can change on both sides at once.
25: The **endoplasmic reticulum** stores calcium that can be released into the cytoplasm through regulated channels. Li and colleagues injected heparin into motor neurons to block **inositol trisphosphate receptors**, or IP3 receptors, one class of intracellular calcium-release channel. They then measured serotonin-dependent EPSP enhancement.

Postsynaptic heparin reduced facilitation below the control level. Other store-related manipulations, including changes to ryanodine receptors, gave the same result. These channels control the intracellular calcium available to the cell, which is distinct from the voltage-gated calcium entry that triggers release at sensory terminals.

Several independent interventions converge on the same calcium-store pathway, with each one timed to the same serotonin exposure. The postsynaptic route from serotonin to enhanced transmission runs through these stores.
26: **Exocytosis** is the fusion of an intracellular membrane compartment with the cell surface. Li and colleagues injected botulinum toxin B into motor neurons to block this process. Blocking exocytosis in the postsynaptic cell targets membrane trafficking there, not transmitter-vesicle fusion in the sensory neuron.

During and after a 10 min serotonin exposure, control synapses showed enhanced EPSPs. Postsynaptic toxin disrupted the lasting component after serotonin was removed. Recordings in the ganglia separated AMPA-type and NMDA-type glutamate-receptor contributions, and the later enhancement involved the AMPA-mediated response.

Calcium-dependent insertion or regulation of postsynaptic AMPA receptors fits these results. Presynaptic release enhancement and postsynaptic receptor regulation can work together, and they differ in onset and persistence.
27: Li and colleagues moved the postsynaptic toxin experiment from culture into a reduced siphon-withdrawal preparation. Repeated siphon taps produced habituation, followed by tail shock and further siphon tests. Identified motor neurons were injected with botulinum toxin B before the behavioral sequence.

Control preparations increased siphon withdrawal after shock, whereas postsynaptic toxin blocked this dishabituation. Motor activity recorded alongside the movement linked the cell-targeted treatment to a measured behavioral change. Vehicle injections and test-only sequences produced no block.

Postsynaptic exocytosis in the siphon motor cells contributes to the behavior. The same requirement is tested in other gill responses and in sensitization protocols, and the intact network around these cells is part of the same account.
28: Montarolo and colleagues cultured identified sensory neurons with the gill motor neuron L7. A single serotonin application produced short-term EPSP enhancement. Five 5 min applications spread over about 1.5 h produced **long-term facilitation**, a persistent increase in transmission that was still present after the training ended.

At 24 h, repeated treatment increased connection strength by about 71%, while a single application left no comparable enhancement. Controls received the same recording and perfusion procedures without the repeated serotonin sequence. The same sensory–motor pair was retested after the delay.

The cellular result reproduces the timing of sensitization, and withdrawal behavior is a separate measure. One application and repeated applications produce different outcomes, so stimulus history is what drives the lasting change at this synapse.
29: Montarolo and colleagues added inhibitors during repeated serotonin treatment to separate immediate facilitation from its persistence. **Translation** makes protein from RNA, whereas **transcription** makes RNA from a DNA template. Anisomycin and emetine block translation, and actinomycin D and α-amanitin block transcription.

The inhibitors prevented the enhancement that is normally retained at 24 h, while short-term facilitation during serotonin exposure remained. Cultures treated with the drugs alone and reapplication tests showed a selective loss of persistence, not a general failure of synaptic transmission. Immediate and delayed responses therefore need different macromolecules.

Preserved short-term facilitation points to something other than neuronal death or a complete block of transmission. Because the synthesis inhibitors act on many products, the experiment identifies synthesis during induction, and the particular proteins involved are identified separately.
30: Montarolo and colleagues changed when anisomycin was present relative to repeated serotonin. A three-hour exposure during and immediately after induction blocked long-term facilitation. Inhibition that began much earlier, or several hours later, left the 24 h enhancement intact.

Biochemical measurements showed strong suppression of protein synthesis during drug exposure and recovery after washout. The timing of the drug therefore lines up with its effect on the cell. Long-term facilitation depends on new synthesis during a restricted induction period.

A **critical window** fits the production of proteins that start or stabilize persistent change. The identities, turnover rates and locations of these proteins are measured by separate experiments, which distinguish somatic transcription from translation near terminals.
31: Bailey and Chen labeled the identified gill motor neuron L7 and the sensory neurons that contact it, then examined the junctions with electron microscopy. Electron micrographs resolved labeled sensory terminals contacting labeled motor-cell processes. Trained and control animals were examined under the same conditions.

Long-term sensitization increased the number of presynaptic contacts onto L7. The change came with a corresponding increase in the size of presynaptic swellings and in active zones, the specialized membrane regions that support release. More contacts provide one anatomical route to stronger total input.

A labeled contact is a structural measure, and its release probability is measured physiologically in the same preparation. The contact addition is linked to the sensitization of the behavior at an identified output cell.
32: **Synapsin** is a protein associated with synaptic vesicles and their organization. Hart and colleagues treated sensory neurons with repeated serotonin and measured synapsin RNA, protein and immunostaining. **Immunostaining** uses antibodies to show where a protein sits within a cell.

Synapsin levels rose after treatment, with brighter staining in sensory-neuron varicosities at 2 h and at 24 h. The time course rose in steps rather than in a steady climb. Measurements in cultured neurons and in nervous tissue placed the rise in presynaptic structures that take part in release.
Synapsin is a candidate effector that links serotonin-dependent gene regulation to persistent changes in synaptic function. Its requirement is tested by knocking it down in the same cultures.
33: **CREB1**, the cAMP response element-binding protein, is a transcription factor that regulates gene expression by binding DNA. A **promoter** is a DNA region that controls transcription of a gene. Hart and colleagues identified a cAMP response element in the _Aplysia_ synapsin promoter, a site that CREB1 can bind.

A promoter-driven fluorescent reporter increased expression after serotonin treatment. Chromatin immunoprecipitation, which pulls down DNA bound to a chosen protein, found more CREB1 bound to the synapsin promoter. These measurements connect the regulatory sequence, transcription-factor binding and expression level in one chain.

Serotonin-dependent signaling therefore reaches synapsin production through CREB1 binding at this promoter. Other transcriptional responses of long-term facilitation are assigned to their own target genes.
34: **Histones** are proteins around which DNA is packaged, and their chemical modifications influence access to regulatory regions. Hart and colleagues examined the synapsin promoter after serotonin treatment with antibodies against CREB1, acetylated histones and histone deacetylase 5. **Acetylation** adds an acetyl group to a protein.

Serotonin increased acetylation of histones H3 and H4 near the promoter and reduced the binding of histone deacetylase 5, an enzyme that removes acetyl groups. CREB1 binding rose in the same region. This pattern favors greater transcriptional access and matches the measured increase in synapsin expression.
The chromatin changes appear alongside the CREB1 binding in the same region of the promoter. The first modification in this sequence is identified by timing experiments.
35: **RNA interference** uses complementary small RNA molecules to reduce expression of a target RNA. Hart and colleagues injected sensory neurons with synapsin-targeting small interfering RNA, or siRNA, and with control siRNA. Serotonin training and EPSP recordings were then carried out in the sensory–motor cocultures.

Targeting synapsin blocked the serotonin-induced rise in its protein and impaired facilitation measured 24 h later. Basal synapsin levels and short-term synaptic responses were measured separately. The knockdown therefore links the induced expression change to the lasting physiological outcome.

Synapsin is required for facilitation under this protocol, and it is one component of persistent enhancement. Vesicle organization, receptor signaling, transcription and synaptic structure interact with it.
36: Lee and colleagues examined **ApCPEB4**, an RNA-binding translation regulator in _Aplysia kurodai_, a related sea-hare species. They attached fluorescent reporters to its 3′ untranslated region, an RNA segment that controls expression without encoding protein sequence.

Severed neurites allowed local responses to be separated from delivery by the cell body. Serotonin increased reporter expression in these isolated processes. Translation-related controls separated this increase from a requirement for new transcription.
Isolated processes hold a local pool of RNA that responds to modulatory signaling without the nucleus. Local translation therefore adds a control point for facilitation alongside transcription.
37: Lee and colleagues reduced ApCPEB4 expression with target-specific double-stranded RNA and recorded EPSPs in cultured sensory–motor pairs. Five serotonin pulses normally induced facilitation measured 24 h later. ApCPEB4 knockdown blocked this enhancement, while control RNA and knockdown of the earlier-described ApCPEB did not.

Overexpressing ApCPEB4 lowered the threshold for persistent enhancement, so one serotonin pulse supported a response that normally required repeated treatment. Fluorescent labeling and expression measurements were taken alongside the recordings, tying the intervention to the intended protein.
ApCPEB4 lacks the prion-like domain of ApCPEB and binds different RNA targets. Its role in starting persistent change is distinct from the maintenance role of ApCPEB.
38: Lee and colleagues asked whether PKA can phosphorylate ApCPEB4 and whether that change affects facilitation. **Phosphorylation** adds a phosphate group and can change a protein's activity or its partners. Biochemical assays and neuronal expression experiments addressed the two parts of this signaling link.

PKA phosphorylated ApCPEB4. Replacing threonine at position 294 with alanine prevented phosphorylation there and interfered with long-term facilitation. Pharmacological treatments that targeted ERK and protein kinase C had different effects from the PKA-sensitive one, which ties a translation-regulatory protein to a kinase already implicated in serotonin-dependent enhancement.
The mutant protein changes more than its phosphorylation site, so it is compared with the wild-type protein in the same cultures. The PKA-to-ApCPEB4 link is shown in the cultured connection.
39: Kassabov and colleagues identified **ApNT**, an Aplysia neurotrophin, and **ApTrk**, its receptor tyrosine kinase. A **neurotrophin** is a secreted signaling protein that regulates neuronal growth or function. Alternative RNA processing produced ApNT isoforms with different processing and secretion properties.

Tagged isoforms were expressed in sensory–motor cultures and examined with biochemical assays and fluorescence microscopy. Their distributions differed between cell bodies, neurites and secretion-related compartments. The labeling connects each isoform's processing to where it sits in the cell.
The ApNT isoform with the stronger secretion profile reaches the ApTrk receptor on distant neurites. Receptor activation in those neurites is then tested with functional assays.
40: Kassabov and colleagues manipulated ApNT–ApTrk signaling in cultured sensory–motor connections. A **dominant-negative receptor** is an altered receptor that interferes with signaling by the normal receptor. Expressing dominant-negative ApTrk impaired serotonin-induced long-term facilitation and left short-term enhancement intact.

Raising ApNT expression increased synaptic strength and increased the number of sensory-neuron varicosities. Confocal images taken over time tracked the structural changes in labeled neuronal processes. Functional EPSPs and growth were measured separately from one another.

Overexpression shows what raised signaling can produce, and receptor interference shows what the training protocol requires. Together these results place a growth-related contribution alongside serotonin, kinase activity and gene-expression mechanisms.
41: Zhou and colleagues injected CREB1-targeting siRNA into sensory neurons and waited 72 h before applying repeated serotonin. The standard protocol used five 5 min pulses of 50 μM serotonin, and EPSPs were recorded before treatment and at 24 h afterward. Control siRNA and vehicle groups were run in parallel.

CREB1 knockdown impaired long-term facilitation. In the reported comparison, control-RNA synapses reached about 184% of their pretest amplitude, whereas CREB1-siRNA synapses reached about 121%. Basal transmission was measured separately in each group.

A transcription factor is therefore needed for persistent synaptic enhancement under this protocol. CREB1 works alongside other regulators, and partial loss of it weakens an otherwise effective training pattern.
42: Zhou and colleagues tested a modified serotonin schedule chosen with a signaling model developed earlier. The recorded EPSPs in sensory–motor cultures are the test, and the model's prediction is secondary. The modified schedule partially restored facilitation after CREB1 knockdown.

**Rolipram** inhibits a cAMP phosphodiesterase, the enzyme that breaks cAMP down. At 0.2 μM, rolipram increased the effect of the modified protocol. Standard training, modified training, vehicle, control RNA and target RNA groups were recorded, so the temporal pattern and the drug can each be assessed.
Rescue was partial, and its size depends on the preparation. Raising cAMP signaling compensates for part of a molecular deficit, and the same recordings identify the neurons in which it occurs.
43: Chen and colleagues imaged labeled sensory–motor cultures repeatedly, before serotonin training and again at 24 h and 48 h afterward. **Reconsolidation** is the process by which a reactivated memory needs renewed stabilization. Reactivation followed by protein-synthesis inhibition reduced the extra varicosities that the earlier training had added.

Following individual structures showed loss of both the original and the newly formed varicosities, not just the serotonin-induced ones. Untrained cultures also showed structural turnover. The final number of swellings therefore reflects turnover in addition to the training effect.

Permanent synapses and stored information are linked through contacts that can be followed one by one. Structural change, physiological transmission and behavioral memory are measured separately before a memory is said to be altered.
44: Chen and colleagues measured siphon-withdrawal duration after long-term sensitization training, pharmacological disruption and later partial retraining. A **latent memory** is a retained consequence of experience that is not evident in the current response but can still shape later performance.

After a kinase-related intervention reduced the expressed sensitization, three additional training bouts restored a long-lasting response. The same short training had no effect in untrained controls. The difference shows a persistent consequence of the earlier experience that survives the loss of its normal expression.

Recovery after retraining points to a retained trace of the original training. The retraining response separates a failure to express sensitization from full elimination of the training-dependent change.
45: Pearce and colleagues tested sensitization while varying protein-synthesis and DNA methyltransferase inhibition. **DNA methyltransferases** add methyl groups to DNA and influence gene regulation. Training, drug timing, retention tests and abbreviated retraining separated initial consolidation, later expression and persistence.

Blocking protein synthesis shortly after training allowed later partial training to recover sensitization, whereas blocking synthesis during training did not. Inhibiting DNA methyltransferase after consolidation reduced the retained response and blocked its recovery by the same short training. Retention was tested over days, not during the initial shock sequence.

Different memory phases depend on different molecular steps. Cellular release, postsynaptic regulation, structural growth and gene regulation each contribute at a different level of this learning system.
